item.title: SSR Mining signs deal to buy Roxmore Resources and its Converse gold project
item.description: SSR Mining Inc. has signed a deal to acquire Roxmore Resources Inc. and its Converse gold project in Nevada in a transaction worth a total of $712 million.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: VANCOUVER — SSR Mining Inc. has signed a deal to acquire Roxmore Resources Inc. and its Converse gold project in Nevada in a transaction worth a total of $712 million. SSR executive chair Rod Antal says the deal represents a compelling opportunity to add a high-quality multi-million-ounce gold resource next door to its Marigold mine at an attractive valuation. Converse is located six kilometres west of SSR Mining’s Marigold complex. For each share they hold, Roxmore shareholders will receive $6.75 in cash plus 0.33 of a share in a new gold exploration company that will hold Roxmore’s Rattlesnake Hills project, Shabu River project and Newton property. The new company, which will be led by members of Roxmore’s current management, will be funded with US$10 million in cash and will be owned 85.01 per cent by former Roxmore shareholders and 14.99 per cent by SSR Mining. Roxmore shares closed at $5.32 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

item.title: IMF raises its forecast for world growth this year but warns of risks from AI boom and debt
item.description: The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including the financial frenzy around ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including the financial frenzy around artificial intelligence. The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1 per cent pace this year. That’s up from its July forecast for 3.0 per cent growth and well below the 3.5 per cent expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4 per cent, it said in its latest Economic Outlook. The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gathered in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3 per cent in 2026 and 2027. Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1 per cent this year, up from 2.0 per cent in 2025, and then slow to 1.9 per cent growth next year, it said. The forecasts are based on a nearly 41 per cent increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7 per cent in 2026, falling to 4.1 per cent next year. They also are based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate. AI has uneven impacts The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks. Its benefits are not shared equally: the U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said. “The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s director of research, told reporters in Bangkok. Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95 per cent of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April. “The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says. Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said. Underscoring such concerns, sell-offs of AI-related shares swept through Asia on Tuesday, with South Korea’s Kospi sinking as much as 7 per cent before it closed 5.5 per cent lower. AI’s effects on employment are another worry, “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. “The impact over time on jobs globally we estimate to be around 40 per cent — jobs either augmented or downgraded or eliminated. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said. Debt remains a key concern for regional economies The IMF chief is urging countries to do a better job of improving their national finances and taming mounting levels of debt. That’s especially crucial at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said. Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7 per cent this year from 4.5 per cent in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4 per cent annual pace. The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions’ economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3 per cent rate of growth in 2027. The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by a meager 1.1 per cent this year and 1.2 per cent in 2027. China, the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5 per cent this year, down from 5 per cent in 2025, in line with the government’s official target. India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7 per cent clip, down from a sizzling 7.7 per cent last year. The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth. ___ Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed. Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

item.title: TC Energy completes Indigenous investment deal in Coastal GasLink
item.description: TC Energy Corp. says it has completed an investment deal that gives five First Nations an economic interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — TC Energy Corp. says it has completed an investment deal that gives five First Nations an economic interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline. Financial terms of the deal were not immediately available. Under the agreement with the FN CGL Pipeline Limited Partnership, the Haisla Nation, Halfway River First Nation, McLeod Lake Indian Band, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations have obtained an economic interest in the entity that holds TC Energy’s limited partner interest in Coastal GasLink. The deal is the first of two planned Indigenous investment transactions related to Coastal GasLink. TC Energy says a second transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year. The company recently announced plans to double the existing capacity of the 670-kilometre Coastal GasLink pipeline, which feeds gas to LNG Canada, by adding new compressor stations and upgrading facilities. The decision came after LNG Canada announced a final investment decision to go ahead with the Phase 2 expansion of its facility in Kitimat, B.C. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

item.title: Americas have glut of heavy oil due to freight squeeze; Asia, Europe scramble for barrels
item.description: Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and U.S. refiners have been running ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: HOUSTON -- Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and U.S. refiners have been running close to their limits. The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above US$100 a barrel. Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many U.S., and some European refineries are typically configured to process. It is usually cheaper than light crude, offering refiners better margins, when shipping costs are affordable. “It’s all freight,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP. Venezuela, the U.S. and Canada all produce more oil than they consume, he said, so they rely on exports to Asia to balance their crude markets. With U.S. diesel prices soaring, the cheap, stranded barrels should be getting snapped up in a diesel-starved market, since heavy crude yields more of the fuel than lighter grades. But Gulf Coast refiners have already bought as much as they can process, analysts and traders said. Venezuelan exports have surged since the U.S. captured former President Nicolas Maduro in January, then started pushing to reactivate the country’s oil sector. Canadian output is at a record and Washington has released more than 130 million barrels from its emergency reserve. The cost of hiring a supertanker from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia, meanwhile, has more than quintupled since February, as ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman tie up vessels worldwide. “You need a ship and the price of ships are going up, and the availability ships are going down,” Shelton said. Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10 a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. Prices for Western Canada Select, excluding shipping or insurance costs, was around $74 on Thursday; Colombia’s main grade Vasconia was trading at around $84; and Ecuador’s Oriente was trading at around $76, Argus said. Venezuelan crude excluding shipping costs was trading around $74.50 a barrel on Thursday, two traders said. Shipping oil on a supertanker from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Europe was estimated to cost around $46 million, or $24.50 a barrel, last week, including ship-to-ship transfer and other costs, according to Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Maritime analyst. That compares with $6.5 million or around $4 a barrel before the Iran war broke out in late February. The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year. U.S. refiners maxed out U.S. refineries have operated at about 93.5 per cent capacity on an average weekly basis so far this year, according to the Energy Information Administration. That is the highest level in 28 years as they crank out as much as fuel as they can to profit from record high diesel prices. While those refineries are complex and geared to run a heavier crude slate, they can only process it up to a certain percentage of their total capacity. “While Venezuela and U.S. emergency barrels have been a factor for months now, leading to near maximum U.S. coker utilization, high freight is now a further headwind to shipping these barrels east and is forcing heavy sour storage builds in the Americas,” Irwin added. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity. Many U.S. refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock. (Reporting by Georgina McCartney and Arathy Somasekhar in Houston and Amanda Stephenson in Calgary; Editing by Liz Hampton, Nathan Crooks and David Gregorio)
